paper_title: GenFirst: Generation Before Reconstruction for Stable End-to-End Latent Generative Modeling

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Latent generative models typically follow a two-stage pipeline, training a variational autoencoder for reconstruction and then a generative model on the frozen latent space. Since reconstruction-optimized latents are not necessarily generation-friendly, jointly training both models is an appealing alternative. However, direct end-to-end training remains challenging, as it is prone to latent collapse and faces a generation-reconstruction conflict. We revisit this problem by analyzing how different objectives shape the latent space and identify two key insights. First, the entropy term in the Kullback-Leibler divergence objective is essential for preventing collapse: reconstruction and prior fitting tend to shrink the posterior, while entropy preserves non-degenerate latent uncertainty. Second, reconstruction and generation exhibit asymmetric learning dynamics: reconstruction is fast and strongly supervised, whereas generation is slower and harder to optimize. Based on these insights, we achieve the first direct end-to-end training without latent collapse and propose GenFirst, a simple generation-before-reconstruction strategy. The generative objective first shapes the latent space under weak reconstruction pressure, after which reconstruction is progressively strengthened to recover visual details. We validate GenFirst with continuous autoregressive priors with exact likelihoods and SiT priors with implicit likelihoods. With our end-to-end objective and GenFirst, SiT achieves a gFID of 0.97 with CFG and 1.45 without CFG on ImageNet-256, while MMDiT reaches a GenEval score of 0.90 on text-to-image generation. Beyond image generation, we extend the framework to shared visual latents for generation and representation learning, and to continuous unified text-image generation. These results demonstrate the generality of stable end-to-end latent learning across generative priors and modalities.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Latent generative models [2, 25, 44, 47, 53, 59, 63, 66, 74, 94] have become dominant paradigm for highresolution image generation. Instead of modeling images directly in pixel space, they first use variational autoencoder (VAE) [38] or visual tokenizer to compress raw pixels into low-dimensional latent space and then train generative model on this latent distribution. Such two-stage pipeline greatly reduces modeling 1 Figure 1 Comparison of latent generative modeling paradigms. (a) Conventional two-stage methods train generative models on fixed, reconstruction-optimized latent space that may be suboptimal for generation. (b) Naïve end-to-end training allows the generative loss to update the encoder but causes latent collapse. (c) REPA-E avoids collapse by stopping generative gradients and reshaping the latent space through an external representation-alignment loss, preventing the generative objective from directly shaping the latent space. (d) Our method enables direct end-to-end training: the prior loss shapes generation-friendly latent space, while the entropy term prevents collapse. complexity and has enabled huge progress in image generation. However, recent works [42, 83, 85, 90, 91] show that VAE latent space optimized for reconstruction is not necessarily optimal for generation. Reconstruction tends to preserve instance-level details, making the latent distribution overly dispersed and harder for generative models to fit and sample from. This mismatch between reconstruction and generation has motivated diverse approaches, including improved autoencoders [83], representation alignment [85], pixel-space generation [5, 43, 49, 86, 93], and end-to-end training [14, 42, 90]. Despite their different designs, these approaches all address shared question: what representation is best suited for generative modeling? natural solution is to jointly train the VAE and generative model, allowing the generative objective to directly shape the latent space. JetFormer [69] and FARMER [93] use invertible normalizing flows [20, 87] instead of VAEs, while SimFlow [90] jointly trains VAE and normalizing flow with fixed VAE variance. REPA-E [42] jointly trains diffusion models with VAE, but observes severe latent collapse when gradients from the generative model are propagated to the VAE. It therefore stops the diffusion gradient and instead uses representation alignment for indirect supervision. Together, these designs highlight the promise of end-to-end latent generative modeling, while leaving its feasibility and optimization mechanism unclear. In this paper, we therefore ask the first fundamental question: Is direct end-to-end training of VAEs and generative models feasible? REPA-E [42] observed that naively propagating the generative loss through the VAE causes latent collapse. To answer this question, we revisit end-to-end training from the perspective of the VAE objective and identify previously overlooked priorentropy imbalance (3.1). LDM [59] established practical VAE training recipe widely adopted by modern latent generative models, where small KL weight weakly regularizes the latent space. The KL regularizer in the VAE objective consists of prior-fitting term and negative posterior-entropy term. The former encourages latent samples to match the Gaussian prior, whereas the latter preserves posterior uncertainty and prevents degeneracy. In naive end-to-end training, the added generative objective introduces strong prior-fitting force, while posterior entropy remains suppressed by the inherited small KL weight. This imbalance drives the posterior variance toward zero and the latent representations toward nearly constant value, ultimately causing latent collapse (5.2). Our analysis turns latent collapse from an empirical failure mode into diagnosable and correctable imbalance in the objective: stable end-to-end training requires explicitly preserving posterior entropy and balancing it against prior fitting. After resolving the collapse issue, end-to-end training still faces generationreconstruction conflict [83]: reconstruction favors preserving instance-specific details, whereas generation favors smoother and more 2 Figure 2 Visualization of the asymmetric learning dynamics between reconstruction and generation. Reconstruction reaches good image fidelity within much fewer training steps, while generation requires longer optimization process to learn sampleable latent distribution. modelable latent distribution, potentially discarding information needed for faithful reconstruction. This results in generationreconstruction trade-off, where improving one objective often degrades the other (3.2). Therefore, we ask second fundamental question: How can we mitigate the generationreconstruction conflict to learn latent space better suited for generative modeling? As shown in figure 2, our experiments reveal asymmetric learning dynamics between reconstruction and generation (3.3). Reconstruction improves rapidly under direct supervision, whereas generation requires longer optimization to learn globally sampleable latent distribution. Strong reconstruction pressure early in training can therefore anchor the encoder to reconstruction-oriented latent space that is difficult for the generative model to learn. Conversely, maintaining excessive generative pressure can limit the recovery of visual details needed for high-quality decoding. These observations suggest that the key is not only how the two objectives are weighted, but also when each objective shapes the latent space. This observation motivates GenFirst, simple generation-before-reconstruction strategy for our end-to-end training framework. Rather than first learning reconstruction-oriented latent space and then forcing the generative model to chase it, GenFirst allows the generative objective to shape the latent distribution early, under weak reconstruction pressure and explicit entropy preservation. Once the latent distribution can be effectively modeled by the generative prior, reconstruction is progressively strengthened to recover visual details. This ordering aligns with the asymmetric learning dynamics of the two objectives: generation needs to shape the latent geometry early, while reconstruction, being faster and more directly supervised, can be strengthened later. We instantiate GenFirst in two representative settings. First, we adopt continuous autoregressive prior from FARMER [93], where exact likelihood is available and the priorentropy balance can be directly analyzed. Second, we apply GenFirst to SiT [47], flow-matching prior with an implicit likelihood, to evaluate whether the strategy generalizes beyond exact-likelihood models. Across class-to-image and text-to-image generation, GenFirst consistently improves the generationreconstruction trade-off, providing practical and reliable recipe for stable end-to-end latent generative modeling. Beyond image generation, we further extend our end-to-end formulation to shared visual latents that support generation, representation learning, and reconstruction. We also apply it to continuous unified textimage modeling, demonstrating its generality across modalities. We summarize our contributions as follows: We identify priorentropy imbalance as the key cause of latent collapse in direct end-to-end training and show that preserving posterior entropy is essential for preventing collapse. We reveal the asymmetric learning dynamics of generation and reconstruction and propose GenFirst strategy that first shapes generation-friendly latent space and then progressively recovers visual details. We validate GenFirst with both exact-likelihood continuous autoregressive priors and SiT-based flowmatching priors, achieving FID of 0.97 on ImageNet and GenEval score of 0.90 on text-to-image generation. We also validate its applicability across objectives and modalities by further experiments.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Latent Generative Models. Latent generative models [2, 25, 44, 47, 53, 59, 63, 66, 92, 94] use image tokenizers, such as VAEs [59, 83], to compress images into lower-dimensional latent space, which simplifies generative modeling while leaving high-frequency details to the tokenizer. However, recent studies [42, 83, 85] show that VAE latent space optimized for reconstruction is not necessarily optimal for generation. Representation Learning for Generation. Recent works explore how to obtain more generation-friendly representations. REPA [85] improves diffusion models by aligning their intermediate hidden states with features from pretrained visual encoders such as DINOv2 [6]. VA-VAE [83] applies representation alignment to VAE training, while REPA-E [42] further propagates the REPA loss through the diffusion model to align the VAE latent space in an end-to-end manner. Another line of work [43, 49, 73, 86, 87, 93] revisits the original pixel representation and removes the VAE entirely. However, pixel-space generative models still face the challenge of modeling high-dimensional data and often remain less efficient than latent generative models. End-to-End Generative Modeling. Several works study joint training of autoencoders and generative models. LSGM [71] jointly trains VAE with score-based generative models using complex design. REPA-E [42] jointly trains VAE and diffusion model by stopping the diffusion gradient to the VAE and introducing representation alignment loss. JetFormer [69] and FARMER [93] jointly train lossless normalizing flows [39, 87] and autoregressive models [63] to map the data distribution to latent distribution modeled by AR priors. SimFlow and MIMFlow [12, 90] jointly train VAE and normalizing flows by fixing the VAE variance. Unified Latents [27] first jointly learns bitrate-controlled latents with an encoder, diffusion prior, and decoder, then freezes the encoder and retrains larger generation-oriented latent diffusion prior for efficient, high-quality synthesis. However, existing works still lack systematic understanding of direct end-to-end training between VAEs and generative models, especially the cause of latent collapse, the conflict between generation and reconstruction in shaping the latent space, and simple general training strategy. In this paper, we revisit end-to-end latent generative modeling from the VAE objective, identify prior-entropy imbalance as the key cause of collapse, and propose generation-before-reconstruction strategy.

sections.title: 3.1 Prior-Entropy Imbalance Causes Latent Collapse
sections.content: To understand why naive end-to-end training collapses, we revisit the KL term. For the standard Gaussian prior p0(z) = (0, I), the KL divergence can be decomposed as DKL(qϕ(zx)p0(z)) = Eqϕ[log qϕ(zx) log p0(z)] = Eqϕ[ log p0(z)] (cid:123)(cid:122) (cid:125) prior fitting (cid:124) H(qϕ(zx)) (cid:123)(cid:122) (cid:125) entropy (cid:124) . (4) (5) The prior-fitting term pulls latent samples toward high-probability regions of the reference prior p0(z). The entropy term counteracts this effect by keeping the posterior from degenerating into point masses. As described above, naive end-to-end training treats the VAE KL loss as an engineering regularizer and keeps the same tiny weight following LDM [59], typically 106. This overlooks the entropy-preserving role of the KL term when learned prior loss is introduced. Once the generative objective is added, it introduces additional prior-fitting pressure and breaks the balance between prior fitting and posterior entropy: λprior + λKL λKL. This priorentropy imbalance drives the posterior variance toward zero and pushes the posterior means to collapse to nearly the same code, resulting in collapsed latent space. Based on this analysis, we explicitly separate prior fitting and posterior entropy in equation (3), and use Lprior to denote the generative objective that shapes the latent distribution: LE2E = λrecLrec + λLPIPSLLPIPS + λGANLGAN + λpriorLprior λentH(qϕ(zx)). (6) In this view, the entropy term is not minor regularizer, but rather provides counteracting force to learned prior fitting and prevents latent collapse. To further illustrate how different losses affect the latent space, we visualize two statistics: Std(µ) and E[σ2]. Std(µ) measures how widely the posterior means are distributed across images, while E[σ2] measures the average posterior uncertainty. As shown in figure 3, different objectives push the latent posterior in different directions. When reconstruction dominates, Std(µ) increases but E[σ2] decreases: images become easier to reconstruct, but the latent space contains gaps between codes and may be difficult to sample from. When prior fitting dominates without sufficient entropy, both Std(µ) and E[σ2] decrease, causing the posterior to collapse toward nearly constant code. Adding the entropy term increases E[σ2], increases posterior overlap and reduces gaps between sampled codes, which prevents collapse and improves sampleability. Additionally, we discuss subtle shortcut solution behind the collapse behavior in section B.

sections.title: 3.2 Generation--Reconstruction Trade-off
sections.content: After preventing latent collapse with entropy, end-to-end training still faces generationreconstruction conflict. To study this conflict, we keep the reconstruction-related loss weights the same as in the VAE training setting and vary only the prior loss weight. As shown in figure 5(a), increasing λprior improves generation but hurts reconstruction: gFID improves from 120.60 to 8.06, while rFID worsens from 0.53 to 4.20. This suggests that generation and reconstruction favor different operating points along the observed trade-off and cannot generally reach their individual optima at one prior weight. We analyze this problem using the continuous autoregressive log pθ(ziz<i)]. prior from FARMER [93], where the exact likelihood is available: LAR prior = Ezqϕ(zx) [ (cid:80) 5 (a) Latent dim (b) VAE size (c) Prior size Figure 4 Larger latent dimension, VAE capacity, and prior capacity for balancing generation and reconstruction. This setting allows us to directly control the strength of the generative objective. We then explore three natural strategies to mitigate this conflict, but find that they still fail to resolve it. Increasing the latent dimension. We first increase the latent dimension to relax the information bottleneck [83]. As shown in figure 4a, larger latent dimensions can tolerate stronger prior weights, but the improvement is limited: even increasing the dimension from 16 to 128 only supports λprior 0.1 before reconstruction deteriorates. Moreover, larger latent dimension makes the AR prior harder to model. Thus, increasing latent dimension shifts the trade-off but does not remove the generationreconstruction conflict. Scaling the VAE. We next test whether stronger VAE can recover details from more generation-friendly latent space. Compared with the default VAE (block = 2), we increase both encoder and decoder depth (block = 4), or increase only the decoder depth. As shown in figure 4b, scaling the VAE does not alleviate the conflict and can even hurt reconstruction, suggesting that simply increasing VAE capacity is insufficient. Scaling the generative model. Finally, we scale the AR model size to better fit complex latent distributions. As shown in figure 4c, larger prior improves generation but further degrades reconstruction, indicating stronger shaping pressure on the latent space. Therefore, scaling the prior can amplify the dominance of the generation objective rather than resolving the conflict.

sections.title: 3.3 Loss Balancing Is Not Enough
sections.content: The above results show that increasing the latent dimension, scaling the VAE, or scaling the generative model does not remove the generationreconstruction conflict. We next examine whether better loss balancing can alleviate it. As shown in figure 5(a), the prior loss weight λprior strongly affects this trade-off. We therefore test several common weighting schemes with simple tuning, including constant weighting, cosine decay, and PI-style adaptive control [62]. However, table 2 shows that none consistently achieves satisfactory balance, highlighting the difficulty of dynamically balancing the two objectives. To understand this failure, we revisit the asymmetric learning dynamics between reconstruction and generation. As shown in figure 2, reconstruction is fast and strongly supervised mapping problem: given latent samples, the decoder receives direct supervision from the target images and can quickly recover visual details. In contrast, generation is slower distribution-modeling problem: the prior must learn the global latent distribution before it can produce realistic samples. Therefore, reconstruction can reach good image fidelity within far fewer training steps, whereas generation requires substantially longer training to produce recognizable samples. Based on this observation, we propose generation-before-reconstruction training strategy (GenFirst), which treats the conflict as an optimization-order problem rather than pure loss-balancing problem. GenFirst lets the generative prior shape generation-friendly latent space and then strengthens reconstruction to recover visual details within the latent space.

sections.content: Motivated by the asymmetric learning dynamics discussed in section 3.3, we propose generation-beforereconstruction (GenFirst), two-stage schedule based on the same end-to-end objective in equation (6). Throughout training, we keep the reconstruction, LPIPS, and GAN weights unchanged from standard VAE training, and tie the entropy weight to the prior weight, i.e., λent = λprior. (12) In the generation-first stage, the stronger generative objective plays the main role in shaping generationfriendly latent space, while reconstruction preserves image information and posterior entropy prevents latent collapse. In the reconstruction-refinement stage, we reduce the prior and entropy weights so that reconstruction receives greater relative influence and recovers visual details without substantially disrupting the generationfriendly latent space formed in the first stage. In practice, we use longer generation-first stage for latent-space formation and shorter reconstruction-refinement stage for recovering visual details. Unlike cosine schedules or PI-style adaptive weighting [62], GenFirst does not merely adjust loss magnitudes; it explicitly separates latent-space formation from reconstruction refinement according to the asymmetric learning dynamics of generation and reconstruction.

sections.title: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Architecture configurations, dataset details, and stage-specific optimization details are provided in section C.1. Datasets and metrics. We evaluate class-conditional generation on ImageNet [18] at 256 256 and 512 512 resolutions. For text-to-image generation, we train on publicly available datasets [13, 15, 16, 18, 35, 51, 54], and evaluate on GenEval [24] and DPG-Bench [31]. For ImageNet generation, we report gFID [28], Inception Score (IS) [60], Precision, and Recall [40] using 50K generated samples. For reconstruction, we report rFID, PSNR [33], LPIPS [89], and SSIM [77]. EAR. EAR combines the VAE architecture from MAR [44], using the 16d16 latent setting, with the continuous autoregressive prior from FARMER [93]. The VAE and AR prior are jointly trained from scratch using our end-to-end objective with GenFirst. We set λprior = λent = 1 for the 500-epoch generation-first stage and reduce both weights to 0.25 for the 140-epoch reconstruction-refinement stage. We use batch size of 512 and linearly warm up the learning rate to 1 104 during the first 10 epochs, then keep it constant. EiT. EiT denotes our diffusion-based instantiation of the end-to-end framework. We use SiT [47] for classconditional ImageNet generation and MMDiT [22] for text-to-image generation. Following REPA-E [42], training consists of an end-to-end phase followed by prior-only phase. During the end-to-end phase, the VAE and SiT are jointly optimized using our end-to-end objective with GenFirst. We set λprior = λent = 0.1 for the 80-epoch generation-first stage and reduce both weights to 0.01 for the 40-epoch reconstruction-refinement stage. During the prior-only phase, we freeze the VAE and train SiT for an additional 800 epochs. Other optimization settings follow REPA-E [42]. High-resolution generation. For both EAR and EiT, we reuse the VAE trained at 256 256 resolution and freeze it. We then train only the corresponding AR or SiT generative prior at 512 512 resolution. Text-to-image generation. We use the same two-phase training protocol for text-to-image generation. During the end-to-end phase, we consider two variants. Version jointly trains SiT-XL/2 and the FLUX.1-dev VAE on ImageNet using the same end-to-end protocol as class-conditional EiT. Version jointly trains MMDiT-L/2 [22] and the FLUX.1-dev VAE directly on the text-to-image training data. During the prior-only phase, we freeze the resulting VAE and train the target MMDiT-XL/2 on the text-to-image dataset. Following UniDDT [75] and PixelGen [50], we train MMDiT at 256 256 for 200K steps and then at 512 512 for 80K steps. sections.title: 5.2 Analysis
sections.content: For ease of analysis, unless otherwise specified, we use the exact-likelihood EAR as the default setting, and report gFID and IS without guidance. Does end-to-end training learn generation-friendly latent space? We compare four protocols in table 1: Frozen VAE is the standard two-stage baseline; Naive E2E propagates the generative loss to the VAE without explicit entropy preservation; Stable E2E uses our entropy-preserving objective and GenFirst strategy; and Frozen E2E-trined VAE freezes the VAE learned by our Stable E2E objective with GenFirst and trains new prior from scratch. Naive E2E collapses for both EAR and SiT, whereas Stable E2E remains stable. More importantly, replacing the reconstruction-trained VAE with the frozen E2E-trained VAE substantially improves newly trained prior: gFID decreases from 36.33 to 5.67 for EAR and from 7.90 to 3.57 for SiT. These results show that stable end-to-end training learns more generation-friendly latent space. EAR and SiT exhibit different behaviors during joint training. For EAR, the tractable likelihood directly models the VAE latent density, so Stable E2E slightly outperforms retraining the prior on the frozen E2E-trained VAE. In contrast, SiT lacks an explicit likelihood over VAE latents, making joint VAESiT optimization less effective than freezing the E2E-trained VAE and training new SiT prior. We replace the FLUX.1-dev VAE [3] encoder with the Vision Transformer (ViT) [21] from Qwen3-VL [1] followed by dimension-reduction projector that predicts the posterior mean and variance. We randomly initialize the decoder, freeze the encoder, and first train the decoder for 100K steps for image reconstruction before end-to-end training. In the first setting (figure 9(a)), we directly impose representation supervision on the latent representation. Specifically, we apply SigLIP loss [70, 88] across samples within each batch together with classification-based supervision loss [32] on the latent features. This design allows the representation-learning objective to directly shape the same latent representation used by the generative model. In the second setting (figure 9(b)), we use the intermediate ViT features from the encoder for representation supervision. We feed these visual features together with the corresponding image captions into Qwen3-VL and minimize the negative log-likelihood (NLL) of the caption tokens [68]. Unlike contrastive learning, which typically benefits strongly from large batch sizes due to its reliance on in-batch negatives, this objective is independent of cross-sample comparisons. As shown in table 9, end-to-end training with the generative objective alone achieves an ImageNet linear-probe accuracy of 77.71. Adding latent-level SigLIP supervision improves the accuracy to 79.25, while slightly improving generation and reconstruction, reaching 0.90 GenEval, 83.76 DPG-Bench, and 0.39 rFID. VLMNLL supervision yields substantially larger semantic improvement, increasing linear-probe accuracy to 81.69, which exceeds the 79.64 accuracy of the pretrained Qwen3-VL ViT. Meanwhile, it largely preserves generative performance, achieving 0.89 GenEval and 83.49 DPG-Bench, with only moderate change in reconstruction quality. These results show that representation supervision can be incorporated into our end-to-end framework while largely preserving the generation-friendly properties of the learned latent space. We further investigate whether our end-to-end formulation can extend beyond image latents to jointly model text and images. As shown in figure 9(c), we encode text into continuous latent representations with text VAE and reconstruct the original text through decoder using cross-entropy (CE) loss. We then feed both text and image latents into block-causal MMDiT [22] and train text-to-image p(it) and image-to-text p(ti) generation. The block-causal MMDiT uses the same model scale as the MMDiT-XL/2 in our text-to-image experiments. The diffusion objectives from both directions shape the latent representations, while the entropy term prevents latent collapse. We apply the same GenFirst strategy to balance latent modeling and reconstruction. Due to computational constraints, the end-to-end phase uses only half as many training steps as our text-to-image experiment, while the subsequent prior-only phase uses only 30.8% of its text-to-image training samples. We initialize the text VAE from Cola [26] and first replace the frozen text VAE with its end-to-end trained counterpart while keeping the image VAE frozen. As shown in table 10, this improves GenEval from 79.88 to 81.87 and DPG-Bench from 63.96 to 68.24, while also substantially improving image-to-text generation, with CIDEr increasing from 20.03 to 30.19. Consistent improvements are also observed across BLEU-4, METEOR, ROUGE-L, SPICE, and CLIPScore. The qualitative comparisons in figure 10 show the same trend: end-to-end trained latents improve prompt fidelity in text-to-image generation and produce more coherent and accurate captions in image-to-text generation. These results show that end-to-end latent learning extends beyond images and can jointly improve continuous text and image representations within unified generative model.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We revisit end-to-end training of VAEs and generative models and make two key observations. First, we find that latent collapse in naive end-to-end training is mainly caused by prior-entropy imbalance. Second, we identify asymmetric learning dynamics underlying the generationreconstruction conflict. Based on these observations, we introduce an entropy-preserving end-to-end objective that enables stable direct joint training and further propose GenFirst, generation-before-reconstruction strategy that mitigates the generation reconstruction conflict. Experiments show that our method learns more generation-friendly latent spaces and improves the generationreconstruction trade-off. We hope this work provides simple and practical recipe for stable end-to-end latent generative modeling.

sections.title: 7 Limitations
sections.content: Although GenFirst enables stable end-to-end training and substantially alleviates the generationreconstruction conflict, it does not completely eliminate the trade-off. The end-to-end trained VAE therefore still sacrifices some reconstruction fidelity, as reflected by metrics such as PSNR. Further improving reconstruction while preserving generation-friendly latent space remains an important direction for future work. Additionally, EAR is limited by the current CFG strategy for continuous autoregressive models. Without CFG, scaling the EAR prior consistently improves gFID, whereas gFID with CFG does not improve accordingly. Developing stronger guidance methods for continuous autoregressive models is therefore left for future work. Finally, our text-to-image experiments use substantially smaller training corpus than large-scale text-to-image models. Scaling the data and training budget may further reveal the potential of end-to-end learned latent spaces.

Version performs slightly better overall, while the two variants remain close, indicating that end-to-end VAE training is effective on both ImageNet and text-to-image training data. Effect of end-to-end training on VAE reconstruction. We evaluate the reconstruction quality of different VAEs in table 12. Compared with their corresponding pretrained VAEs, end-to-end trained VAEs show moderate degradation in reconstruction metrics while maintaining strong reconstruction quality overall. In the extreme case, σ2 ϕ(x) 0, µϕ(x) c, where is nearly constant across different images. Since the posterior noise becomes very small, the decoder may still exploit small residual differences in µϕ(x) for reconstruction, even though the overall latent distribution is already highly concentrated. For diffusion or flow-matching prior, such concentrated latent distribution also makes the denoising objective artificially easy. Consider the linear interpolation used by SiT, If the latent collapses to c, then zt = (1 t)ϵt + tz, = ϵt. zt (1 t)ϵt + tc, zt 1 . Therefore, predicting the target velocity requires little knowledge of the image distribution: the model can approximately recover the target through simple affine transformation of the noisy input around the nearly constant code c. The denoising loss can thus become small even though the generative model has not learned meaningful latent distribution. This explains why preserving posterior entropy is important during end-to-end training. Increasing the entropy prevents σ2 ϕ(x) from vanishing. Under non-trivial posterior noise, if all posterior means were also nearly identical, the latent samples of different images would become indistinguishable to the decoder. The reconstruction objective therefore encourages µϕ(x) to remain image-dependent and distributed across the latent space. Together, entropy preservation and reconstruction discourage both variance and mean collapse. Motivated by this observation, we tie the entropy weight to the prior weight in our default end-to-end objective, λent = λprior. This keeps posterior-entropy preservation coupled to the strength of prior-fitting pressure and avoids the degenerate shortcut observed in naive end-to-end training.

sections.content: C.1 Training and Inference Details We provide the complete architecture, training, and inference configurations for EAR, EiT, and text-to-image EiT in tables 15 to 17. Below, we summarize the training pipeline and the relationship between different resolutions and model variants. EAR on ImageNet. The detailed EAR configuration is provided in table 15. For ImageNet 256 256, we jointly train the MAR VAE [44] and the continuous AR prior [93] from scratch using the two-stage GenFirst schedule. The resulting VAE is then reused for the resolution 512 512 experiment: we keep the VAE frozen and train larger EAR prior on the higher-resolution latent sequences. Therefore, the resolution 512 512 experiment evaluates whether the latent space learned by GenFirst at resolution 256 256 transfers to higher-resolution generative modeling without further adapting the tokenizer. We follow FARMER [93] for the continuous-AR parameterization and resampling-based classifier-free guidance. EiT on ImageNet. The ImageNet EiT configuration is summarized in table 16. At ImageNet 256 256, training consists of an end-to-end phase followed by prior-only phase. During the end-to-end phase, the VAE and SiT are jointly optimized using the two-stage GenFirst schedule. We then freeze the resulting VAE and train new SiT on its latent space. For resolution 512 512, we directly reuse and freeze the VA-VAE obtained from the resolution 256 256 end-to-end stage, and train only new SiT at the higher resolution. We observe that the latent space changes rapidly during end-to-end training, which can leave the decoder insufficiently adapted to the updated latents. Therefore, for the ImageNet-256 EiT results in table 6 only, we additionally fine-tune the VAE decoder for 10K steps after the end-to-end stage. This improves the 80-epoch unguided gFID from 3.00 to 2.79. This decoder fine-tuning is not used in the other EiT experiments. For the corresponding 80-epoch guided result, we use CFG scale 2.0 with guidance interval of [0.2, 0.85]. Unless otherwise specified, the optimization and REPA settings follow REPA-E [42]; complete architecture, training, and inference configurations are provided in table 16. Text-to-image EiT. We consider two variants for obtaining an end-to-end trained FLUX.1-dev VAE [3], as detailed in table 17. In Version A, the VAE is jointly trained with smaller MMDiT (MMDiT-L/2) directly on the text-to-image training data using GenFirst. In Version B, the VAE is jointly trained with SiT-XL/2 on ImageNet using the same GenFirst setting as class-conditional EiT. These variants compare VAE shaped directly by text-conditioned generation with one shaped by class-conditional ImageNet generation. After the end-to-end phase, we freeze the resulting VAE and train the same MMDiT-XL/2 prior for both variants. We first train at 256 256 for 200K steps, continue at 512 512 for 80K steps, and finally fine-tune on the OpenAI-4o dataset [13] at 512 512 for 40K steps. Complete architecture, optimization, and inference settings are provided in table 17. C.4 Unified Text--Image Modeling via End-to-End Diffusion As discussed in section 5.4, our end-to-end formulation is not restricted to image latents and can be applied to other modalities. We therefore extend our framework to text and jointly model text and images within single diffusion backbone, allowing the generative objective to shape both text and image latent spaces. Text latent representation. We initialize the text VAE from Cola [26]. Each text token is encoded into 16-dimensional continuous latent, and the decoder reconstructs the original tokens with cross-entropy loss. We train the encoder and decoder trunks together with the latent projections (194M trainable parameters), while freezing the token embedding and output vocabulary head. The encoder applies non-affine LayerNorm to the posterior mean, so we do not apply the additional latent normalization used for image latents. To handle variable-length captions efficiently, text sequences are packed without padding and converted to dense (B, L, d) representation with validity mask only before entering the diffusion model. Block-causal joint diffusion. During the end-to-end phase, we jointly model text and image latents using block-causal MMDiT-L/2 [22] with 24 blocks, width 1024, 16 attention heads, and patch size 2. The model maintains separate streams for the two modalities and couples them through joint attention. At 256 256 resolution, each image contains 16 16 = 256 latent tokens, while text contains at most 256 latent tokens and is partitioned into blocks of 16 tokens. Image tokens use bidirectional attention, whereas text tokens use block-causal attention, enabling block-wise generation of p(ti). We train text-to-image p(it) and image-to-text p(ti) with equal sampling probability. For each sample, only the target modality is noised and supervised by the diffusion objective, while the conditioning modality is kept clean at = 0. Image timesteps are sampled independently per example, whereas text timesteps are sampled independently for each text block. For text generation, each noisy block attends to all preceding clean blocks and to the noisy tokens within the current block, allowing all blocks to be trained in parallel with clean prefix conditioning. Cross-modal attention is direction-dependent: image tokens attend to clean text for p(it), while text tokens attend to clean image features for p(ti). For classifier-free guidance, we drop the conditioning modality with probability 0.1 by disabling the corresponding cross-modal attention. Training objective. The text VAE follows the same end-to-end formulation as the image branch: Ltext = LCE + λKLDKL(qϕt(ztx) (0, I)) λentH(qϕt(zx)) + λpriorLprior, (17) where Lprior is the flow-matching objective of the joint diffusion model and λKL = 106. Following our analysis in section 3.1, the entropy term counteracts the prior-fitting pressure and prevents latent collapse. We apply the entropy term to modality only when it is generated, since clean conditioning modality does not receive prior-fitting pressure from the diffusion objective. For text-only end-to-end training, the image VAE remains frozen and only the text encoder receives generative gradients. For joint end-to-end training, both text and 23 image VAEs are optimized under the same GenFirst schedule, allowing the bidirectional diffusion objectives to shape both latent spaces. Training and evaluation. We compare three latent-training settings. In the first setting, both the Cola text VAE and the FLUX.1-dev image VAE [3] are kept frozen, providing fully frozen latent baseline. In the second setting, we end-to-end train the text VAE together with the block-causal MMDiT while keeping the FLUX.1-dev image VAE frozen, isolating the effect of reshaping the text latent space. In the third setting, both the Cola-initialized text VAE and the FLUX.1-dev image VAE are jointly optimized with the block-causal MMDiT, allowing the bidirectional generative objectives to reshape both latent spaces. End-to-end training is conducted at 256 256 resolution on the same dataset as our text-to-image experiments, with captions truncated to 256 tokens. We use batch size of 256, AdamW [46] with learning rates of 104 for MMDiT and 105 for the text VAE, and gradient clipping at 1.0. We use λprior = λent = 0.1 for the first 200K steps and reduce both to 0.01 for another 100K steps. For joint end-to-end training, the same GenFirst schedule is applied to both text and image latent optimization. After end-to-end latent training, we freeze the resulting text and image VAEs and train new block-causal MMDiT-XL/2 from scratch. The prior-only model uses 28 blocks, width 1152, and 16 attention heads, matching the model scale of MMDiT-XL/2 in our main text-to-image experiments. We follow the same training protocol as our text-to-image experiments: 200K steps at 256 256, 80K steps at 512 512, followed by 40K steps of fine-tuning on GPT-4o data. We evaluate text-to-image generation using GenEval and DPG-Bench. We evaluate image-to-text generation on the COCO Karpathy test split using CIDEr, BLEU-4, METEOR, ROUGE-L, SPICE, and CLIPScore.
